list.listitem: Consider rickets in the differential diagnosis of a child presenting with failure to thrive, developmental delay, and the bony abnormalities of bowing limbs, fractures, frontal bossing of the head, and widened joints. C
Consider osteomalacia in an adult with fractures, bone pain, back pain, and weakness. Treat symptomatically. C
Treatment depends on the underlying cause (nutritional or inherited, vitamin D dependent or resistant). C
Burosumab is a monoclonal antibody approved for X-Linked hypophosphatemic rickets in adults and children ≥1 year of age. It is administered subcutaneously every 2 weeks. B

background.definition: Rickets is the failure of growing bones to mineralize properly; osteomalacia is the failure of adult bones to mineralize properly.

list.listitem: The estimated prevalence of nutritional rickets is 5 cases per 1 million children aged 6 months to 5 years in the United States.
Osteomalacia is present in approximately 8.0% of elderly patients with hip fractures.
Vitamin D deficiency, a risk factor for the development of osteomalacia, may occur in approximately one third of elderly patients in developed countries.
A meta-analysis of identified 1725 cases of tumor induced osteomalacia (TIO) and concluded that it is more common in men, who are also more likely to have associated fractures.
Nutritional deficiencies are the most common cause of rickets worldwide.
Most cases of nutritional rickets in the United States are in dark-skinned individuals.
Up to 10% of elderly patients with fractures are diagnosed with osteomalacia.
An association with comorbid high lead levels has been described in China.
Vitamin D deficiency may be due to inadequate nutritional intake; kidney, gastrointestinal, parathyroid, or liver disease; or inadequate sunlight exposure.
Inherited disorders of vitamin D metabolism include vitamin D-dependent and vitamin D-resistant rickets.
Calcium and phosphorous deficiencies lead to abnormal bone formation.

Malignancy and exposure to certain medications (some antacids, anticonvulsants, steroids, and diuretics) or inhibitors of calcification (excess fluoride, aluminum) may lead to abnormal bone formation.

Proper bone formation requires a complex interplay of several organ systems (skin, liver, kidney, gastrointestinal tract, parathyroid) and substrates (particularly vitamin D, calcium, phosphorous, parathyroid hormone).
Any disturbance in the functioning of these organs or in the quantities of substrates results in the lack of calcified osteoid in osteomalacia and the build-up of unossified cartilage in rickets.
Humans maintain adequate levels of vitamin D by absorption from the gut or production from cholesterol.

Vitamin D production begins in the skin with ultraviolet light, which aids in the conversion of 7-dehydrocholesterol to cholecalciferol (vitamin D3). It is then converted to calcidiol via the liver and enzyme vitamin D3-25 hydroxylase; calcidiol is then converted to calcitriol via the kidney and enzyme 25(OH)D3-1-alpha hydroxylase.

Vitamin D-dependent rickets is autosomally inherited. Type I is due to deficiency of renal 25(OH)D3-1-alpha hydroxylase. Type II is due to the defective interaction between cacitriol and its receptor.

Vitamin D-resistant rickets include X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets or autosomal recessive or dominant inherited hypophosphatemic rickets with hypocalciuria; both types involve impaired proximal renal tubular reabsorption of phosphorous. PHEX gene mutation causing FGF23 [ fibroblast growth factor 23] excess is the most common genetic form of X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Limited sunlight exposure (UVB).For example, excessive sunscreen use, whole body clothing due to cultural and regious reasons
Diet low in vitamin D, calcium, or phosphorous
Exposure to certain medications (some antacids, anticonvulsants, steroids, and diuretics) or inhibitors of calcification (excess fluoride, aluminum)
Genetic variants near genes involved in cholesterol synthesis, hydroxylation, and vitamin D transport

list.listitem: Screening is not routinely recommended, although physicians in low income countries where malnourishment is more common should consult local guidelines and practice. C
Vitamin D supplementation is recommended for at-risk infants. B
The Endocrine Society guidelines (2024) recommend against screening or checking vitamin D levels.
Case-finding in malnourished infants in low income countries should be considered, though.
Targeted screening of high-risk infants (ie, dark-skinned infants who have been breastfed and living in northern climates) with wrist radiographs and vitamin D levels has been suggested.

A systematic review found four studies with 1700 participants that evaluated vitamin D supplementation to prevent rickets. Two of the studies reported a reduced risk of rickets (relative risk 0.04 in a Turkish study and 0.76 in a Chinese study), while two studies of older children found no benefit. Information regarding cost-effectiveness is lacking.
There are no established screening guidelines for osteomalacia in the elderly patient.

The Endocrine Society guidelines (2024) did not find research to support achieving a specific vitamin D level and did not identify a demographic group that must receive vitamin D. However, there are some groups that may benefit from assuring a daily intake of vitamin D through fortified foods or vitamin D supplementation, including children and adolescents, as well as adults who are pregnant, have impaired glucose tolerance, or are older than 74 years.
Provide 400 IU of vitamin D per day to all infants who do not consume at least one liter per day of vitamin D-fortified formula. C
Provide 400 IU of vitamin D per day to all older children who are ingesting less than one liter per day of vitamin D-fortified milk. C
Provide 400 IU of vitamin D per day to all adolescents who do not obtain 400 IU of vitamin D per day through vitamin D-fortified milk (100 IU per 8-oz serving) and vitamin D-fortified foods. C

Nutrition guidelines for bone health from the Institute of Medicine are for 400 IU of vitamin D per day for North Americans and up to 800 IUs for people over age 70 years. Calcium requirements are 500 milligrams of calcium per day for children ages 1 through 3 years; 800 milligrams daily for those ages 4 through 8 years and for women ages 19 through 50 years and men up to 71 years; 1,000 milligrams per day on average for women over age 50 years and men over age 71 years; and 1,300 milligrams per day for adolescents.

Typical features of rickets include growth retardation; weakness; tetany; and bony deformities of bowing limbs, fractures, frontal bossing of the head, and widened joints. Osteomalacia is often asymptomatic. C
Useful laboratory tests include serum calcium (total and ionized), phophorous, calcidiol, alkaline phosphatase, parathyroid hormone, creatinine, and urinary calcium and phosphorus levels. C
Obtain radiographs of fast-growing skeletal areas in children and symptomatic areas in adults. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Persistent rhinitis, rash, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, anemia, and maternal history of the illness
Otherwise normal physical examination and laboratory and radiographic studies

Otherwise normal laboratory studies and physical examination; characteristic radiograph of tibia reveals widening of the medial growth plate and flattening of the medial aspect of the proximal epiphysis
Bruising, unusual skin markings, retinal hemorrhages, and normal laboratory studies
Normal calcium, phosphorous, and alkaline phosphorous levels
Otherwise normal physical examination and laboratory findings, symptoms localized to affected bone

list.listitem: Key elements of the history: family and personal history of musculoskeletal abnormalities, gestational age, diet, sunlight exposure, parental consanguinity, and exposure to medications that may inhibit calcification (certain antacids, anticonvulsants, steroids, and diuretics).
Key elements of the physical examination: bony deformities (bowing limbs, fractures, widened joints, frontal bossing of the head), poor dentition, alopecia.
In a systematic review, hypocalcemic convulsions was the most common symptom among children less than age 1 year and bowed legs was the most common characteristic for children age 1 or older.
Developmental delay and bony abnormalities in a dark-skinned, solely breastfed infant may be indicative of rickets.

Osteomalacia may present without any symptoms or obvious abnormal physical examination findings, but it must be included in the differential diagnosis of a patient with pain (commonly back pain) and weakness.
Typical findings in different types of rickets are shown below:
Rickets: Typical radiographic findings include widening of the distal physis, fraying and widening of the metaphysis, and angular deformities of the arm and leg bones.

Nutritional rickets: Patients usually have low serum calcium, phosphorous, calcidiol, and low urinary calcium levels; they also have high serum parathyroid hormone and alkaline phosphatase levels, and high urinary phosphorous levels.

Osteomalacia: Patients have low serum calcium, phosphorous, and calcidiol levels, and high serum alkaline phosphatase and parathyroid hormone. However, hypocalcemia and hypophosphatemia are poor predictors of osteomalacia; the presence of increased alkaline phosphatase is helpful but may increase false-positive results. Radiographic findings may include osteopenia, fractures, Looser zone abnormalities (perpendicular radiolucent lines), or indistinct or concave vertebral bodies. Bone bioipsy may be needed if tests are inconclusive in patients with suspected osteomalacia.

Identification of culprit tumors causing osteomalacia: A systematic review reported a pooled sensitivity of 73% for tumor detection using F-18 FDG PET/CT. Somatostatin receptor-based imaging modalities such as Ga-68 DOTATOC PET/CT are very sensitive.
If rickets is suspected, determine serum calcium (total and ionized with serum albumin), phosphorous, alkaline phosphatase, parathyroid hormone, urea nitrogen, creatinine, and calcidiol levels.
Perform urinalysis and determine urinary levels of calcium and phosphorous.
Obtain radiographs of rapidly growing skeletal areas in children, such as knee or wrist, and of any symptomatic bony areas in adults.
A multidiciplinary approach involving the endocrinologist, nephrologist, geneticist, and orthopedists is needed to provide comprehensive care and the best possible outcomes.
Nutritional rickets is treated by replacing the deficient nutrient either in a single large IM dose or in smaller daily doses for 12 weeks, accompanied by daily calcium supplementation.C
Type I vitamin D-dependent rickets is treated with calcitriol and type II vitamin D-dependent rickets is treated with massive doses of calcitriol and calcium. C
Treat vitamin D-resistant rickets (if X-linked) with oral phosphate and calcitriol; autosomal recessive and dominant types are treated with oral phosphate alone. C
Osteomalacia is treated supportively with pain control; any underlying nutritional or systemic disease should be treated aggressively. C
Burosumab is a monoclonal antibody approved for X-Linked hypophosphatemic rickets in adults and children ≥1 year of age. It is administered subcutaneously every 2 weeks. B

Vitamin D deficiency: Various vitamin D preparations, doses (high vs low), dosing schedules (single vs multiple doses), and administration routes (oral vs IM) are available for use depending on patient compliance, tolerability, and preference. If compliance is concern, a single IM injection of vitamin D preparation is recommended.

Nutritional rickets: Options include a daily dose of vitamin D for 12 weeks (<12 mos, 2000 IU; 12 mos to 12 yrs, 3000-6000 IU; or 12 years and older, 6000 IU) or a single large dose, also called stoss therapy (<3 mos not recommended, 3 to 12 mos 50,000 IU IM, 12 mos to 12 yrs 150,000 IU IM; 12 years and older, 300,000 IU IM). Following treatment, a maintenance dose of 400 to 600 IU/day is recommended. Patients should receive concomitant 500 mg calcium daily during treatment.
Doses greater than 300,000 IU are more likely to lead to hypercalcemia.
Nutritional rickets and type II vitamin D-dependent rickets: oral calcium.
Nutritional deficiency and vitamin D-resistant rickets: phosphorous.
Vitamin D-dependent rickets and types I and II and X-linked vitamin D-resistant rickets: calcitriol.
In a meta-analysis, authors were unable to find evidence of benefit of recombinant human growth hormone therapy to improve linear growth for children with X-linked hypophosphatemia.

In 2018, the FDA approved a medication for X-Linked hypophosphatemic rickets called burosumab for adults and children ≥1 year of age. Burosumab is a recombinant human IgG1monoclonal antibody that binds to and inhibits the activitiy of FGF23 and is administered subcutaneously every 2 weeks. If burosumab is unavailable, conventional treatment with oral phosphate and active Vitamin D analogues (alfacalcidol or calcitiol) to correct and/or prevent bone deformation is recommended.
Orthopedic procedures are sometimes necessary to correct bony deformities and manage fractures.
Ensure that the patient is receiving the recommended daily allowances (RDAs) of calcium and phosphorous.
RDAs vary by age. Calcium ranges from 210 mg per day for infants to 1300 mg per day for lactating women. Phosphorus ranges from 100 mg per day in infants to 1250 mg per day in lactating women.
Refer patients to a nephrologist or gastroenterologist if a kidney, liver, or gastrointestinal cause is suspected.
Refer patients with severe bony deformities or fractures to an orthopedic surgeon for definitive treatment.
Consider hospitalization while the evaluation is proceeding if child abuse is suspected.
Serum chemistries and radiographic changes typically normalize within 6 months of beginning treatment. C
Monitor serum calcium, phosphorus, alkaline phosphatase, and calcidiol levels, as well as urine calcium, urine phosphorous, and the spot urine calcium-to-creatinine ratio. C
The earliest biochemical change after the initiation of treatment of rickets is a rise in the level of phosphorous, then a rise in the level of calcium within the first week.
Radiographic changes in patients with rickets can occur within a week, and physical examination findings may normalize within 6 months.
Treatment with vitamin D and calcium will normalize serum chemistries (ie, PTH) as soon as 3 to 5 months after beginning treatment for osteomalacia secondary to vitamin D deficiency.

Some serum chemistries (such as 1,25(OH)2D and phosphorus) may begin to normalize as soon as 1 to 3 days after tumor removal in cases of tumor-induced osteomalacia. Within 3 months, complete resolution of osteomalacia may be confirmed by bone biopsy.
After treatment is initiated, monitor serum calcium, phosphorous, alkaline phosphatase, and calcidiol levels.
Also monitor urinary calcium and phosphorous levels.
Mother's of breastfed infants with rickets, especially those presenting with hypocalcemic seizures, are likely to have severe vitamin D deficiency (<20 ng/mL) warranting testing and treatment.
Recommend a healthy diet.
Ensure adequate vitamin D intake.
